claim: The elongating ribosome is an efficient helicase.
source: Although the elongating ribosome is an efficient helicase, certain mRNA stem-loop structures are known to impede ribosome movement along mRNA and stimulate programmed ribosome frameshifting via mechanisms that are not well understood.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge about ribosome function.

claim: Certain mRNA stem-loop structures impede ribosome movement along mRNA.
source: Although the elongating ribosome is an efficient helicase, certain mRNA stem-loop structures are known to impede ribosome movement along mRNA and stimulate programmed ribosome frameshifting via mechanisms that are not well understood.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge.

claim: Certain mRNA stem-loop structures stimulate programmed ribosome frameshifting.
source: Although the elongating ribosome is an efficient helicase, certain mRNA stem-loop structures are known to impede ribosome movement along mRNA and stimulate programmed ribosome frameshifting via mechanisms that are not well understood.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge.

claim: Frameshift-inducing stem-loops from E. coli dnaX mRNA strongly inhibit A-site tRNA binding.
source: We find that upon encountering the ribosome, the stem-loops strongly inhibit A-site tRNA binding and ribosome intersubunit rotation that accompanies translation elongation.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the biochemical and smFRET experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Frameshift-inducing stem-loops from HIV gag-pol transcript strongly inhibit A-site tRNA binding.
source: We find that upon encountering the ribosome, the stem-loops strongly inhibit A-site tRNA binding and ribosome intersubunit rotation that accompanies translation elongation.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the biochemical and smFRET experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Frameshift-inducing stem-loops inhibit ribosome intersubunit rotation that accompanies translation elongation.
source: We find that upon encountering the ribosome, the stem-loops strongly inhibit A-site tRNA binding and ribosome intersubunit rotation that accompanies translation elongation.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the smFRET experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: The HIV stem-loop docks into the A site of the ribosome.
source: Electron cryo-microscopy (cryo-EM) reveals that the HIV stem-loop docks into the A site of the ribosome.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the cryo-EM analysis described in the manuscript.

claim: mRNA stem-loops can transiently escape the ribosome helicase by binding to the A site.
source: Our results suggest that mRNA stem-loops can transiently escape the ribosome helicase by binding to the A site.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the cryo-EM and biochemical data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Stem-loops can modulate gene expression by sterically hindering tRNA binding.
source: Thus, the stem-loops can modulate gene expression by sterically hindering tRNA binding and inhibiting translation elongation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing inhibition of tRNA binding.

claim: Stem-loops can modulate gene expression by inhibiting translation elongation.
source: Thus, the stem-loops can modulate gene expression by sterically hindering tRNA binding and inhibiting translation elongation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing inhibition of translation.

claim: The mRNA channel of the bacterial small ribosomal subunit accommodates 11 nucleotides downstream of the first (+1) nucleotide of the P-site codon.
source: In the bacterial ribosome, the mRNA channel accommodates 11 nucleotides downstream of the first (+1) nucleotide of the P-site codon (Takyar et al., 2005; Yusupova et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: The ribosome is a processive helicase that unwinds three basepairs per translocation step.
source: The ribosome was shown to be a processive helicase, which unwinds three basepairs per translocation step (Qu et al., 2011; Takyar et al., 2005; Wen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Most secondary structure elements within coding regions of mRNAs do not influence the rate of translation elongation.
source: Accordingly, transcriptome-wide ribosome profiling analysis demonstrated that most of the secondary structure elements within coding regions of mRNAs do not influence the rate of translation elongation (Del Campo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a ribosome profiling study.

claim: mRNA stem-loop structures can induce ribosome stalling that results in accumulation of truncated polypeptides.
source: mRNA stem-loop structures can induce ribosome stalling that results in accumulation of truncated polypeptides (Yan et al., 2015) and no-go mRNA decay (Doma and Parker, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: mRNA stem-loop structures can induce no-go mRNA decay.
source: mRNA stem-loop structures can induce ribosome stalling that results in accumulation of truncated polypeptides (Yan et al., 2015) and no-go mRNA decay (Doma and Parker, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The α subunit of the signal recognition particle receptor is co-translationally targeted to the endoplasmic reticulum membrane by a mechanism that requires a translational pause induced by an mRNA stem-loop structure.
source: For example, the α subunit of the signal recognition particle receptor is co-translationally targeted to the endoplasmic reticulum membrane by a mechanism that requires a translational pause induced by an mRNA stem-loop structure (Young and Andrews, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Ribosome pausing induced by mRNA hairpins and pseudoknots accompanies −1 programmed ribosome frameshifting.
source: Ribosome pausing induced by mRNA hairpins and pseudoknots accompanies −1 programmed ribosome frameshifting (PRF), which controls expression of a number of proteins in bacteria, viruses and eukaryotes (Caliskan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: −1 PRF regulates synthesis of DNA polymerase III in bacteria.
source: In particular, −1 PRF regulates synthesis of DNA polymerase III in bacteria (Tsuchihashi and Kornberg, 1990); HIV cytokine receptor CCR5 in higher eukaryotes (Belew et al., 2014); gag-pol proteins in retroviruses, including Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) (Jacks et al., 1988); and C-terminally extended polyprotein in coronaviruses, including SARS-CoV-2, which caused the COVID-19 pandemic (Dinman, 2012; Kelly and Dinman, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: −1 PRF regulates HIV cytokine receptor CCR5 in higher eukaryotes.
source: In particular, −1 PRF regulates synthesis of DNA polymerase III in bacteria (Tsuchihashi and Kornberg, 1990); HIV cytokine receptor CCR5 in higher eukaryotes (Belew et al., 2014); gag-pol proteins in retroviruses, including Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) (Jacks et al., 1988); and C-terminally extended polyprotein in coronaviruses, including SARS-CoV-2, which caused the COVID-19 pandemic (Dinman, 2012; Kelly and Dinman, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: −1 PRF regulates gag-pol proteins in retroviruses, including HIV.
source: In particular, −1 PRF regulates synthesis of DNA polymerase III in bacteria (Tsuchihashi and Kornberg, 1990); HIV cytokine receptor CCR5 in higher eukaryotes (Belew et al., 2014); gag-pol proteins in retroviruses, including Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) (Jacks et al., 1988); and C-terminally extended polyprotein in coronaviruses, including SARS-CoV-2, which caused the COVID-19 pandemic (Dinman, 2012; Kelly and Dinman, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: −1 PRF regulates C-terminally extended polyprotein in coronaviruses, including SARS-CoV-2.
source: In particular, −1 PRF regulates synthesis of DNA polymerase III in bacteria (Tsuchihashi and Kornberg, 1990); HIV cytokine receptor CCR5 in higher eukaryotes (Belew et al., 2014); gag-pol proteins in retroviruses, including Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) (Jacks et al., 1988); and C-terminally extended polyprotein in coronaviruses, including SARS-CoV-2, which caused the COVID-19 pandemic (Dinman, 2012; Kelly and Dinman, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: −1 PRF requires the presence of a heptanucleotide slippery sequence XXXYYYZ.
source: −1 PRF requires the presence of two signals in an mRNA: the heptanucleotide slippery sequence XXXYYYZ (where X and Z can be any nucleotide and Y is either A or U) and a downstream frameshift stimulating sequence (FSS).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the requirements for −1 PRF.

claim: −1 PRF requires a downstream frameshift stimulating sequence (FSS).
source: −1 PRF requires the presence of two signals in an mRNA: the heptanucleotide slippery sequence XXXYYYZ (where X and Z can be any nucleotide and Y is either A or U) and a downstream frameshift stimulating sequence (FSS).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the requirements for −1 PRF.

claim: The FSS is an RNA hairpin or a pseudoknot.
source: The FSS is an RNA hairpin or a pseudoknot (Atkins et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The slippery sequence allows cognate pairing of the P-site and A-site tRNAs in both 0 and −1 frames.
source: The slippery sequence allows cognate pairing of the P-site and A-site tRNAs in both 0 and −1 frames and thus makes frameshifting thermodynamically favorable (Bock et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: FSSs inhibit the rate of translocation of the A- and P-site tRNAs basepaired with the slippery sequence by at least one order of magnitude.
source: A number of studies have shown that FSSs inhibit the rate of translocation of the A- and P-site tRNAs basepaired with the slippery sequence by at least one order of magnitude (Caliskan et al., 2014; Caliskan et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2014; Kim et al., 2014) and thus produce ribosome pauses (Caliskan et al., 2014; Caliskan et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2014; Kim et al., 2014; Kontos et al., 2001; Lopinski et al., 2000; Somogyi et al., 1993; Tu et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: FSSs produce ribosome pauses.
source: A number of studies have shown that FSSs inhibit the rate of translocation of the A- and P-site tRNAs basepaired with the slippery sequence by at least one order of magnitude (Caliskan et al., 2014; Caliskan et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2014; Kim et al., 2014) and thus produce ribosome pauses (Caliskan et al., 2014; Caliskan et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2014; Kim et al., 2014; Kontos et al., 2001; Lopinski et al., 2000; Somogyi et al., 1993; Tu et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: Translocation through three GC basepairs is only 2 to 3-fold slower than translocation along a single-stranded codon.
source: Single-molecule experiments showed that translocation through three GC basepairs is only 2 to 3-fold slower than translocation along a single-stranded codon (Chen et al., 2013; Desai et al., 2019; Qu et al., 2011), indicating that the stability of the three basepairs adjacent to the mRNA channel has a relatively moderate effect on translocation rate.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous single-molecule studies.

claim: The stability of the three basepairs adjacent to the mRNA channel has a relatively moderate effect on translocation rate.
source: Single-molecule experiments showed that translocation through three GC basepairs is only 2 to 3-fold slower than translocation along a single-stranded codon (Chen et al., 2013; Desai et al., 2019; Qu et al., 2011), indicating that the stability of the three basepairs adjacent to the mRNA channel has a relatively moderate effect on translocation rate.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited single-molecule experiments.

claim: Neither the thermodynamic stability of the entire FSS nor the stability of the basepairs adjacent to the mRNA entry channel fully correlate with the efficiency of frameshifting.
source: Consistent with this idea, neither the thermodynamic stability of the entire FSS nor the stability of the basepairs adjacent to the mRNA entry channel fully correlate with the efficiency of frameshifting (Chen et al., 2009; Hansen et al., 2007; Mouzakis et al., 2013; Ritchie et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The dnaX_Slip mRNA programs −1 PRF with ~60% efficiency.
source: Consistent with previous publications (Caliskan et al., 2017; Kim and Tinoco, 2017; Larsen et al., 1997), we observed a frameshifting efficiency of ~60% (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a measurement from the frameshifting assay shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: When ribosomes are programmed with dnaX_Slip ΔFSS mRNA, the efficiency of −1 PRF decreases to ~25%.
source: When ribosomes were programmed with the truncated dnaX_Slip ΔFSS mRNA, which lacks the FSS (Figure 1), the efficiency of −1 PRF decreased to ~25%, demonstrating that the FSS stimulates ribosome frameshifting.
evidence: This is a measurement from the frameshifting assay shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The FSS stimulates ribosome frameshifting.
source: When ribosomes were programmed with the truncated dnaX_Slip ΔFSS mRNA, which lacks the FSS (Figure 1), the efficiency of −1 PRF decreased to ~25%, demonstrating that the FSS stimulates ribosome frameshifting.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing frameshifting efficiency with and without the FSS.

claim: The NR and R conformations of the ribosome correspond to 0.6 and 0.4 FRET states of S6-cy5/L9-cy3 FRET pair.
source: The NR and R conformations of the ribosome have been shown to correspond to 0.6 and 0.4 FRET states of S6-cy5/L9-cy3 FRET pair (Cornish et al., 2008; Ermolenko et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Ribosomes containing P-site peptidyl-tRNA are predominately in the NR (0.6 FRET) state.
source: Consistent with previous reports, ribosomes containing P-site peptidyl-tRNA (N-Ac-Val-Lys-tRNALys) are predominately in the NR (0.6 FRET) state (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; Cornish et al., 2008; Ermolenko et al., 2007).
evidence: This is observed in the smFRET data shown in Figure 2A and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The transpeptidation reaction and subsequent movement of tRNAs into hybrid states are typically much faster than tRNA binding to the A site.
source: The transpeptidation reaction and subsequent movement of tRNAs into hybrid states are typically much faster than tRNA binding to the A site (Blanchard et al., 2004a; Johansson et al., 2008; Juette et al., 2016; Rodnina and Wintermeyer, 2001; Sharma et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous kinetic studies.

claim: The median τbd for dnaX_Slip mRNA programmed ribosomes is 18.2 s.
source: τbd and τtrl of dnaX_Slip mRNA programmed ribosomes were remarkably long with median values of 18.2 s and 10.7 s, respectively (Figure 2C,E), suggesting inefficient tRNALys binding and translocation.
evidence: This is a measurement from the smFRET data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The median τtrl for dnaX_Slip mRNA programmed ribosomes is 10.7 s.
source: τbd and τtrl of dnaX_Slip mRNA programmed ribosomes were remarkably long with median values of 18.2 s and 10.7 s, respectively (Figure 2C,E), suggesting inefficient tRNALys binding and translocation.
evidence: This is a measurement from the smFRET data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The median τbd for dnaX_Slip ΔFSS mRNA programmed ribosomes is 3.8 s.
source: Median values of τbd (3.8 s) and τtrl (1.5 s) for dnaX_Slip ΔFSS mRNA (Figure 2D,F) were 5- and 7-fold shorter, respectively, than those measured in ribosomes programmed with dnaX_Slip mRNA.
evidence: This is a measurement from the smFRET data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The median τtrl for dnaX_Slip ΔFSS mRNA programmed ribosomes is 1.5 s.
source: Median values of τbd (3.8 s) and τtrl (1.5 s) for dnaX_Slip ΔFSS mRNA (Figure 2D,F) were 5- and 7-fold shorter, respectively, than those measured in ribosomes programmed with dnaX_Slip mRNA.
evidence: This is a measurement from the smFRET data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: dnaX FSS strongly inhibits mRNA/tRNA translocation.
source: In agreement with previously published results (Caliskan et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2014; Choi et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2014), our data demonstrate that dnaX FSS positioned near the mRNA channel entrance strongly inhibits mRNA/tRNA translocation (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the smFRET data shown in Figure 2E,F and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: dnaX FSS strongly inhibits A-site tRNA binding during the elongation cycle.
source: In addition, our data unexpectedly revealed that dnaX FSS also strongly inhibits A-site tRNA binding during the elongation cycle (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the smFRET data shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: When the FSS is positioned one nucleotide away from the entry of mRNA channel, the majority (60%) of ribosomes remain in the NR conformation after addition of EF-Tu•GTP•Tyr-tRNATyr.
source: By contrast, when EF-Tu•GTP•Tyr-tRNATyr was added to ribosomes with the FSS positioned one nucleotide away from the entry of mRNA channel, the majority (60%) of ribosomes remained in the NR conformation (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is observed in the smFRET data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The encounter of the ribosome mRNA entry channel with the FSS inhibits conversion of the ribosome from the NR to R conformation.
source: Hence, the encounter of the ribosome mRNA entry channel with the FSS inhibits conversion of the ribosome from the NR to R conformation, which accompanies tRNA binding.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the smFRET data comparing FSS-containing and ΔFSS mRNAs.

claim: Upon encountering the ribosome, the FSS from HIV stalls the ribosome in the NR conformation.
source: Therefore, similar to the FSS from dnaX, upon encountering the ribosome, the FSS from HIV stalls the ribosome in the NR conformation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the smFRET data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The FSS-induced inhibition of tRNA binding is independent of A-site codon identity.
source: Thus, we show that the FSS-induced inhibition of tRNA binding is independent of A-site codon identity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing results with different A-site codons (UAC and GAG).

claim: In the absence of the slippery sequence, FSS-induced frameshifting is negligible.
source: Therefore, in the absence of the slippery sequence, FSS-induced frameshifting is negligible and does not account for ribosome stalling in the NR conformation observed in the experiments with ribosomes programmed with dnaX_NS or HIV_NS mRNAs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the smFRET data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Pretranslocation-like ribosomes containing deacylated P-site tRNA exhibit similar intersubunit dynamics regardless of whether they are programmed with dnaX_NS, dnaX_NS ∆FSS, HIV_NS or HIV_NS ∆FSS mRNAs.
source: Pretranslocation-like S6-cy5/L9-cy3 ribosomes containing deacylated P-site tRNAPhe exhibited similar intersubunit dynamics regardless of whether they were programmed with dnaX_NS, dnaX_NS ∆FSS, HIV_NS or HIV_NS ∆FSS mRNAs.
evidence: This is observed in the smFRET data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Neither dnaX FSS nor HIV FSS placed near the entry of the mRNA channel directly affect intersubunit dynamics.
source: Hence, neither dnaX FSS nor HIV FSS placed near the entry of the mRNA channel directly affect intersubunit dynamics.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the smFRET data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: dnaX and HIV FSSs do not change the sensitivity of P-site N-Ac-Phe-tRNAPhe toward puromycin.
source: dnaX and HIV FSSs also did not change the sensitivity of P-site N-Ac-Phe-tRNAPhe toward the A-site aminoacyl-tRNA mimic, antibiotic puromycin (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), indicating that the frameshifting-inducing stem-loops placed at the entry of the mRNA channel do not block the transpeptidase activity of the ribosome.
evidence: This is observed in the puromycin assay shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Frameshifting-inducing stem-loops placed at the entry of the mRNA channel do not block the transpeptidase activity of the ribosome.
source: dnaX and HIV FSSs also did not change the sensitivity of P-site N-Ac-Phe-tRNAPhe toward the A-site aminoacyl-tRNA mimic, antibiotic puromycin (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), indicating that the frameshifting-inducing stem-loops placed at the entry of the mRNA channel do not block the transpeptidase activity of the ribosome.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the puromycin assay data.

claim: FSSs from dnaX and HIV likely stall the ribosome in the NR conformation by inhibiting A-site tRNA binding.
source: Therefore, in our smFRET experiments, FSSs from dnaX and HIV likely stall the ribosome in the NR conformation by inhibiting A-site tRNA binding.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the smFRET and puromycin assay data.

claim: In ribosomes programmed with dnaX_NS mRNA, binding of [3H]Tyr-tRNATyr is considerably diminished compared to ribosomes programmed with dnaX_NS ∆FSS mRNA.
source: In ribosomes programmed with dnaX_NS mRNA, binding of [3H]Tyr-tRNATyr was considerably diminished while the incorporation of Val and Phe into the polypeptide chain were only mildly inhibited compared to levels measured in ribosomes programmed with dnaX_NS ∆FSS mRNA lacking the FSS (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is observed in the filter-binding assay shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In ribosomes programmed with HIV_NS mRNA, binding of [3H]Tyr-tRNATyr is strongly inhibited while binding [3H]Phe-tRNAPhe is unaffected.
source: Likewise, in ribosomes programmed with HIV_NS mRNA, binding of [3H]Tyr-tRNATyr was strongly inhibited while binding [3H]Phe-tRNAPhe was unaffected (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is observed in the filter-binding assay shown in Figure 6B.

claim: dnaX FSS reduces the apparent pseudo first order rate of [3H]Tyr-tRNATyr binding to 0.3 min−1.
source: Both dnaX and HIV FSSs dramatically slowed the rate of [3H]Tyr-tRNATyr binding as the apparent pseudo first order rate of tRNA binding was reduced to 0.3 and 0.1 min−1, respectively (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a measurement from the kinetic filter-binding assay shown in Figure 6C.

claim: HIV FSS reduces the apparent pseudo first order rate of [3H]Tyr-tRNATyr binding to 0.1 min−1.
source: Both dnaX and HIV FSSs dramatically slowed the rate of [3H]Tyr-tRNATyr binding as the apparent pseudo first order rate of tRNA binding was reduced to 0.3 and 0.1 min−1, respectively (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a measurement from the kinetic filter-binding assay shown in Figure 6C.

claim: dnaX and HIV FSSs strongly inhibit A-site tRNA binding but do not completely block it.
source: These kinetic experiments also show that while dnaX and HIV FSSs strongly inhibit A-site tRNA binding, they do not completely block it.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the kinetic filter-binding assay data.

claim: Extending the P-site-FSS spacer from 11 to 12 nucleotides increases the apparent pseudo first order rate of [3H]Tyr-tRNATyr binding from 0.1 to 0.4 min−1.
source: Extending the P-site-FSS spacer from 11 to 12 nucleotides increased the apparent pseudo first order rate of [3H]Tyr-tRNATyr binding to the A site of the ribosome from 0.1 to 0.4 min−1 (Figure 6D), however A-site binding remained severely inhibited relative to the ΔFSS control.
evidence: This is a measurement from the kinetic filter-binding assay shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Lengthening the P-site-FSS spacer to 13 nucleotides relieves the FFS-induced inhibition of A-site binding.
source: By contrast, lengthening the P-site-FSS spacer to 13 nucleotide relieved the FFS-induced inhibition of A-site binding as the rate of [3H]Tyr-tRNATyr binding became too fast to be measured by manual mixing kinetic measurements (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is observed in the kinetic filter-binding assay shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Both dnaX and HIV FSSs inhibit A-site tRNA binding only when positioned 11 or 12 nucleotides downstream of the P-site codon.
source: Hence, consistent with smFRET experiments, the filter-binding assay demonstrates that both dnaX and HIV FSSs inhibit A-site tRNA binding only when positioned 11 or 12 nucleotides downstream of the P-site codon.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the filter-binding assay data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: In the absence of EF-Tu, FSSs from dnaX and HIV inhibit non-enzymatic binding of N-Ac-[3H]Tyr-tRNATyr to the A site.
source: Additionally, we found that in the absence of EF-Tu, FSSs from dnaX and HIV also inhibit non-enzymatic binding of N-Ac-[3H]Tyr-tRNATyr to the A site of ribosomes programmed with dnaX_NS mRNA or HIV_NS mRNA (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is observed in the filter-binding assay shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The FSS-induced inhibition of A-site tRNA binding is independent of the EF-Tu function.
source: Therefore, the FSS-induced inhibition of A-site tRNA binding is independent of the EF-Tu function.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the non-enzymatic tRNA binding assay.

claim: FSS-induced binding inhibition of cognate aminoacyl-tRNA to the A site is largely independent of identities of either A- or P-site codons.
source: In addition, we observed that FSS-induced inhibition of cognate aminoacyl-tRNA binding to the A site is largely independent of identities of either A- or P-site codons (Figure 7).
evidence: This is observed in the filter-binding assay shown in Figure 7.

claim: When positioned 11–12 nucleotides downstream of the first nucleotide of the P-site codon, the FSSs from HIV and dnaX mRNAs can substantially inhibit binding of aminoacyl-tRNA to the A site of the ribosome.
source: Taken together, our smFRET and filter-binding experiments indicate that when positioned 11–12 nucleotides downstream of the first nucleotide of the P-site codon, the FSSs from HIV and dnaX mRNAs can substantially inhibit binding of aminoacyl-tRNA to the A site of the ribosome.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the smFRET and filter-binding assay data.

claim: An 11–12 nucleotide distance from the P-site codon corresponds to positioning of the FSSs at the entry of the mRNA channel.
source: Assuming that dnaX and HIV mRNA are threaded through the 30S mRNA channel, an 11–12 nucleotide distance from the P-site codon corresponds to positioning of the FSSs at the entry of the mRNA channel.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known structure of the ribosome and mRNA channel.

claim: The dnaX FSS placed 12 nucleotides downstream from the P-site codon interacts with ribosomal proteins uS3, uS4, and uS5 located at the 30S mRNA entry channel.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, a recent cryo-EM reconstruction revealed that the dnaX FSS placed 12 nucleotides downstream from the P-site codon interacts with ribosomal proteins uS3, uS4, and uS5 located at the 30S mRNA entry channel (Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous cryo-EM study.

claim: Maximum-likelihood classification of the cryo-EM data revealed predominant ribosome states that contained strong density in both the P and A sites.
source: Maximum-likelihood classification of a 640,261-particle data set revealed predominant ribosome states that contained strong density in both the P and A sites, which we interpreted as P-site tRNA and the FSS hairpin, respectively (64% particles total) (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM data analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Two cryo-EM classes comprise the ribosome in classical NR states with P/P tRNA.
source: Two classes comprise the ribosome in classical NR states (NR-I and NR-II,~1° 30S rotation) with P/P tRNA (Figure 8A, Figure 8—figure supplement 2A), while one class represents a R ribosome state with P/E tRNA (R-I,~7° 30S rotation) (Figure 8B, Figure 8—figure supplement 2B), at overall resolutions between 3.1 Å and 3.4 Å.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 8A and Figure 8—figure supplement 2A.

claim: One cryo-EM class represents a R ribosome state with P/E tRNA.
source: Two classes comprise the ribosome in classical NR states (NR-I and NR-II,~1° 30S rotation) with P/P tRNA (Figure 8A, Figure 8—figure supplement 2A), while one class represents a R ribosome state with P/E tRNA (R-I,~7° 30S rotation) (Figure 8B, Figure 8—figure supplement 2B), at overall resolutions between 3.1 Å and 3.4 Å.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 8B and Figure 8—figure supplement 2B.

claim: There is no density at the entry site of the mRNA channel in the cryo-EM structures.
source: By contrast, there is no density at the entry site of the mRNA channel, indicating that the HIV FSS does not bind to the mRNA entry channel.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures.

claim: The HIV FSS does not bind to the mRNA entry channel.
source: By contrast, there is no density at the entry site of the mRNA channel, indicating that the HIV FSS does not bind to the mRNA entry channel.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the absence of density at the mRNA entry channel in the cryo-EM structures.

claim: P-site tRNA is base paired with mRNA in the cryo-EM structures, indicating the absence of frameshifting.
source: P-site tRNA is base paired with mRNA, indicating the absence of frameshifting.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 8C,D.

claim: In all three cryo-EM classes (NR-I, NR-II and R-I), density allows for the distinction of purines from pyrimidines, revealing Watson-Crick pairing between N-Ac-Phe-tRNAPhe and an in-frame UUC codon.
source: In all three classes NR-I, NR-II and R-I, density allows for the distinction of purines from pyrimidines (Figure 8C,D), revealing Watson-Crick pairing between N-Ac-Phe-tRNAPhe and an in-frame UUC codon.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 8C,D.

claim: In the absence of the slippery sequence, dnaX and HIV FSSs do not promote frameshifting.
source: This is consistent with smFRET data showing that in the absence of the slippery sequence, dnaX and HIV FSSs do not promote frameshifting (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is consistent with the smFRET data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: In both NR-I and NR-II structures, the P-site tRNA elbows are shifted by 11.8 Å and 13.0 Å towards the E site compared to P-site tRNA in other classical states.
source: In both NR-I and NR-II structures, the P-site tRNA elbows are shifted by 11.8 Å and 13.0 Å towards the E site compared to P-site tRNA in other classical states (corresponding to tRNA rotation by 18.5° and 21.0°, respectively compared to PDBID: 4V5D, Figure 8E).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Similar tRNA states were observed in several termination complexes where they are thought to represent an intermediate to the P/E hybrid-state after deacylation by a release factor.
source: Similar tRNA states were observed in several termination complexes where they are thought to represent an intermediate to the P/E hybrid-state after deacylation by a release factor (Graf et al., 2018; Svidritskiy et al., 2019; Figure 8—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous cryo-EM studies.

claim: The position of the tRNA CCA tail in the 50S peptidyl-transferase center is similar to that in the peptidyl-tRNA complexes.
source: Nevertheless, the position of the tRNA CCA tail in the 50S peptidyl-transferase center is similar to that in the peptidyl-tRNA complexes (Polikanov et al., 2014), suggesting that NR-I and NR-II can be sampled with peptidyl-tRNAs.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures and supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The FSS hairpin stacks on the purine-rich GAG codon and linker nucleotides AAGAU to occupy the ribosomal A site.
source: Instead of binding next to the mRNA channel, the FSS hairpin stacks on the purine-rich GAG codon and nucleotides AAGAU (nucleotides 59–63 of HIV (GAG) NS mRNA between GAG and the FSS), which we further refer to as the linker sequence, to occupy the ribosomal A site (Figure 9A–C).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 9A–C.

claim: No additional density is observed that could correspond to the acceptor stem of A-site tRNA in the cryo-EM structures.
source: In both the R and NR states, no additional density is observed that could correspond to the acceptor stem of A-site tRNA.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures.

claim: Extended portions of the tRNA elbow and acceptor stem would clash with the A-site finger of the 50S subunit.
source: Furthermore, extended portions of the tRNA elbow and acceptor stem would clash with the A-site finger of the 50S subunit (Figure 9A, Figure 8—figure supplement 2D,E) because the density is rotated by ~15° towards the A-site finger (NR-I) compared to A-site tRNA in the classical state (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is observed by modeling tRNA into the cryo-EM density as shown in Figure 9A and Figure 8—figure supplement 2D,E.

claim: In the R-I conformation, the hairpin density merges with the A-site finger density suggesting that the hairpin loop comes into closer contact with the A-site finger.
source: In the R-I conformation, the hairpin density merges with the A-site finger (helix38) density suggesting that the hairpin loop (A75-A78) comes into a closer contact with the A-site finger (helix 38) (Figure 9D) and does not correspond to a hybrid-state A/P tRNA.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 9D.

claim: The interpretation of the cryo-EM density rules out tRNA in A site and explains inhibition of A-site tRNA binding by the presence of the FSS hairpin.
source: Thus, our interpretation of the density rules out tRNA in A site and explains inhibition of A-site tRNA binding by the presence of the FSS hairpin.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cryo-EM structural analysis.

claim: The local resolution of the A site allows to distinguish the major and minor grooves of the A-form RNA.
source: The local resolution of the A site allows to distinguish the major and minor grooves of the A-form RNA, but individual basepair locations cannot be determined, suggesting that the FSS hairpin samples an ensemble of conformations.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM density.

claim: The FSS hairpin samples an ensemble of conformations.
source: The local resolution of the A site allows to distinguish the major and minor grooves of the A-form RNA, but individual basepair locations cannot be determined, suggesting that the FSS hairpin samples an ensemble of conformations.
evidence: This is inferred from the inability to determine individual basepair locations in the cryo-EM density.

claim: The second and third positions of the A-site codon and the linker form an A form-like purine stack.
source: Accordingly, we modeled the second and third positions of the A-site codon and the linker as an A form-like purine stack (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is a model built based on the cryo-EM density shown in Figure 9B.

claim: A kink in the density suggests that one nucleotide in the purine stack, possibly A60, is flipped out of the helix.
source: A kink in the density suggests that one nucleotide in the purine stack, possibly A60, is flipped out of the helix.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM density.

claim: Conformational heterogeneity of the hairpin observed in the cryo-EM structures is likely important for the hairpin's mechanism of action.
source: Conformational heterogeneity of the hairpin observed in our cryo-EM structures is likely important for the hairpin's mechanism of action.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed conformational heterogeneity.

claim: To allow FSS hairpin entry into the A site, the mRNA linker has to be released from the mRNA channel in the 30S subunit.
source: To allow FSS hairpin entry into the A site, the mRNA linker has to be released from the mRNA channel in the 30S subunit.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cryo-EM structure showing the hairpin in the A site.

claim: Dynamic occupancy of the A site by the FSS hairpin may allow an incoming tRNA to eventually overcome the translational block that the hairpin imposes on the ribosome.
source: Dynamic occupancy of the A site by the FSS hairpin may allow an incoming tRNA to eventually overcome the translational block that the hairpin imposes on the ribosome.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed conformational heterogeneity.

claim: FSSs from E. coli dnaX and HIV mRNAs appear to act via the same mechanism due to similar hairpin structures.
source: Although the sequences of these mRNA elements are different, they appear to act via the same mechanism due to similar hairpin structures.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the behavior of dnaX and HIV FSSs in the experiments.

claim: When positioned 11–12 nucleotides downstream of the P-site codon, the FSSs perturb translation elongation through two parallel pathways: inhibiting tRNA binding to the A site and inhibiting ribosome translocation.
source: We found that when positioned 11–12 nucleotides downstream of the P-site codon, the FSSs perturb translation elongation through two parallel pathways: (i) inhibiting tRNA binding to the A site of the ribosome and (ii) inhibiting ribosome translocation (Figure 10).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the smFRET and biochemical data, illustrated in Figure 10.

claim: The observations support the idea that FSSs stimulate frameshifting by pausing the ribosome.
source: These observations support the idea that FSSs stimulate frameshifting by pausing the ribosome.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The finding that the dnaX FSS slows the rate of ribosome translocation by ~10 fold is in agreement with previous reports.
source: Our finding that the dnaX FSS slows the rate of ribosome translocation by ~10 fold is also in agreement with a number of previous reports (Caliskan et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2014; Choi et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2014; Kim and Tinoco, 2017).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the smFRET data and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The data provide no evidence that dnaX and HIV FSSs induce a unique conformation of the ribosome with a 'super-rotated' orientation of ribosomal subunits.
source: While dnaX and HIV FSSs dramatically perturb the kinetics of the elongation cycle, our data provide no evidence that these stem-loops induce a unique conformation of the ribosome with a 'super-rotated' orientation of ribosomal subunits reported previously (Qin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the smFRET data.

claim: In the smFRET study using ribosomes programmed with dnaX_Slip mRNA, only fluctuations between 0.4 and 0.6 FRET states were detected while no FRET states below 0.4 were observed.
source: In our smFRET study using ribosomes programmed with dnaX_Slip mRNA, we only detected fluctuations between 0.4 and 0.6 FRET states corresponding to R and NR conformations while no FRET states below 0.4 were observed.
evidence: This is observed in the smFRET data.

claim: A 5-fold decrease of the rate of Lys-tRNALys binding to the second Lys codon of the dnaX slippery sequence was induced by the FSS.
source: In our work, we observed a 5-fold decrease of the rate of Lys-tRNALys binding to the second Lys codon of the dnaX slippery sequence induced by the FSS (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a measurement from the smFRET data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The rate of tRNA binding decreased by another order of magnitude when the slippery sequence of dnaX mRNA was replaced with non-slippery codons.
source: Furthermore, the rate of tRNA binding decreased by another order of magnitude when the slippery sequence of dnaX mRNA was replaced with non-slippery codons (Figures 3 and 6).
evidence: This is observed in the smFRET and filter-binding assay data shown in Figures 3 and 6.

claim: A-site tRNA inhibition was also observed with the HIV FSS in the context of non-slippery codons.
source: A-site tRNA inhibition was also observed with the HIV FSS in the context non-slippery codons (Figures 4, 5 and 7), suggesting a common underlying mechanism employed by a variety of FSSs.
evidence: This is observed in the smFRET and filter-binding assay data shown in Figures 4, 5 and 7.

claim: The observation of FSS-dependent inhibition of A-site tRNA binding helps to resolve some inconsistencies in previous studies.
source: Our observation of FSS-dependent inhibition of A-site tRNA binding helps to resolve some inconsistencies in previous studies.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the current results with previous studies.

claim: One previous smFRET study suggests that the rate of A-site tRNA delivery during decoding of the slippery sequence of dnaX mRNA is unaffected by the presence of downstream FSS.
source: One previous smFRET study suggests that the rate of A-site tRNA delivery during decoding of the slippery sequence of dnaX mRNA is unaffected by the presence of downstream FSS (Kim et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Other single-molecule experiments suggest that Lys-tRNALys accommodation during decoding of the second Lys codon of dnaX slippery sequence is delayed.
source: Other single-molecule experiments suggest that Lys-tRNALys accommodation during decoding of the second Lys codon of dnaX slippery sequence is delayed (Chen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Two-fold inhibition of A-site codon decoding induced by the FSS was observed when the dnaX slippery sequence was replaced with non-slippery Lys codons AAGAAG.
source: Two-fold inhibition of A-site codon decoding induced by the FSS was observed in another study when the dnaX slippery sequence was replaced with non-slippery Lys codons AAGAAG (Caliskan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: When positioned 11–12 nucleotides downstream of the P-site codon, FSSs likely inhibit A-site tRNA binding and ribosome translocation by sampling two alternative conformations on the ribosome.
source: When positioned 11–12 nucleotides downstream of the P-site codon, FSSs likely inhibit A-site tRNA binding and ribosome translocation by sampling two alternative conformations on the ribosome (Figure 10), consistent with our observation of conformational heterogeneity of the hairpin in the A site.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cryo-EM and biochemical data, illustrated in Figure 10.

claim: In one FSS conformation, the FSS interacts with the mRNA entry channel.
source: In one FSS conformation, which was previously seen in a cryo-EM reconstruction of dnaX-ribosome complex (Zhang et al., 2018), the FSS interacts with the mRNA entry channel.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous cryo-EM study.

claim: Upon encountering mRNA secondary structure the ribosome translocates through two alternative (fast and slow) pathways.
source: It has been recently demonstrated that upon encountering mRNA secondary structure the ribosome translocates through two alternative (fast and slow) pathways (Desai et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The interactions of FSSs with the mRNA entry channel may increase the flux through the slow translocation pathway.
source: The interactions of FSSs with the mRNA entry channel may increase the flux through the slow pathway and thus decrease the average rate of ribosome translocation (Desai et al., 2019).
evidence: This is speculation based on the previous study cited.

claim: In another FSS conformation, nucleotides between the P site and the FSS disassociate from the mRNA channel, and the HIV FSS docks into the A site.
source: In another FSS conformation, which was visualized by our single-particle cryo-EM analysis, nucleotides between the P site and the FSS disassociate from the mRNA channel, and the HIV FSS docks into the A site thus sterically hindering tRNA binding.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures.

claim: The linker sequence between the A-site codon and the FSS may facilitate binding of the FSS into the A site.
source: The linker sequence between the A-site codon and the FSS may facilitate binding of the FSS into the A site.
evidence: This is speculation based on the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The homo-purine sequence encompassing the second and third positions of the A-site codon and the linker form a purine stack.
source: Our structure suggests that the homo-purine sequence encompassing the second and third positions of the A-site codon and the linker form a purine stack.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The formation of an A-form like single-stranded helix by the linker nucleotides may make the release of the mRNA nucleotides from the mRNA channel and docking of the FSS into the A site more thermodynamically favorable.
source: The formation of an A-form like single-stranded helix by the linker nucleotides may make the release of the mRNA nucleotides between P-site codon and FSS from the mRNA channel and docking of the FSS into the A site more thermodynamically favorable.
evidence: This is speculation based on the cryo-EM structure.

claim: A short four-basepair-long hairpin was observed in the A site of the ribosome bound to a short model mRNA (MF36) derived from phage T4 gene 32 mRNA.
source: A short four-basepair-long hairpin was observed in the A site of the ribosome bound to a short model mRNA (MF36) derived from phage T4 gene 32 mRNA (Yusupova et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous crystallographic study.

claim: The hairpin following the start codon may facilitate initiation of translation of gene 32.
source: Crystallographic analyses suggested that the hairpin following the start codon may facilitate initiation of translation of gene 32 (Yusupova et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous crystallographic study.

claim: A short five-basepair-long hairpin of the bacteriophage T4 gene 60 was visualized by cryo-EM in the A-site of the ribosome stalled at the 'take-off' mRNA site containing a stop codon.
source: Another short five-basepair-long hairpin of the bacteriophage T4 gene 60 was visualized by cryo-EM in the A-site of the ribosome, which was stalled at the 'take-off' mRNA site containing a stop codon (Agirrezabala et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous cryo-EM study.

claim: The hairpin prevents binding of the release factor 1 (RF1), thus inhibiting translation termination and inducing translational bypassing.
source: The hairpin prevents binding of the release factor 1 (RF1), thus inhibiting translation termination and inducing translational bypassing (Agirrezabala et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous cryo-EM study.

claim: A short two-basepair-long hairpin was observed in the A site of the ribosome in which the P and A sites were occupied by an inhibitory codon pair CGA-CCG that causes ribosome stalling.
source: Another short two-basepair-long hairpin was observed in the A site of the ribosome in which the P and A sites were occupied by an inhibitory codon pair CGA-CCG that is known to cause ribosome stalling (Gamble et al., 2016; Tesina et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Occlusion of the A site by RNA stem-loops may be a common strategy shared by many regulatory stem-loops.
source: These observations suggest that occlusion of the A site by RNA stem-loops may be a common strategy shared by many regulatory stem-loops.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the current findings with previous observations of hairpins in the A site.

claim: −1 PRF can occur through three different pathways: slippage of the single P-site tRNA when the A site remains vacant, frameshifting of both A-site and P-site tRNAs during aa-tRNA accommodation to the A site, and slippage of A- and P-site tRNAs during translocation.
source: Several lines of evidence suggest that −1 PRF can occur through three different pathways: (i) slippage of the single P-site tRNA when the A site remains vacant, (ii) frameshifting of both A-site and P-site tRNAs during aa-tRNA accommodation to the A site, and (iii) slippage of A- and P-site tRNAs during translocation (Dinman, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous review.

claim: −1 PRF on both dnaX and HIV mRNAs involves P-site tRNA slippage and frameshifting during translocation of two tRNAs.
source: A number of studies indicated that −1 PRF on both dnaX and HIV mRNAs involves P-site tRNA slippage and frameshifting during translocation of two tRNAs, that is pathways (i) and (iii) (Brunelle et al., 1999; Caliskan et al., 2017; Jacks et al., 1988; Korniy et al., 2019a; Léger et al., 2007; Yelverton et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: Partitioning between frameshifting pathways is modulated by tRNA abundance.
source: Partitioning between these pathways is modulated by tRNA abundance (Caliskan et al., 2017; Korniy et al., 2019a; Korniy et al., 2019b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The observation that frameshift-inducing hairpins inhibit both A-site tRNA binding and mRNA translocation is consistent with single tRNA slippage and translocation frameshifting pathways.
source: Our observation that frameshift-inducing hairpins inhibit both A-site tRNA binding and mRNA translocation are consistent with single tRNA slippage (i) and translocation (iii) frameshifting pathways, respectively.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Transient binding of FSS stem-loops to the A site of the ribosome may mediate frameshifting in insertion sequences of the IS1-IS3 family of bacterial transposable elements.
source: Likewise, transient binding of FSS stem-loops to the A site of the ribosome may mediate frameshifting in insertion sequences of the IS1-IS3 family of bacterial transposable elements (Chandler and Fayet, 1993) and orf 1a/1b of astroviruses (Marczinke et al., 1994).
evidence: This is speculation based on the current findings and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Transient binding of FSS stem-loops to the A site of the ribosome may mediate frameshifting in orf 1a/1b of astroviruses.
source: Likewise, transient binding of FSS stem-loops to the A site of the ribosome may mediate frameshifting in insertion sequences of the IS1-IS3 family of bacterial transposable elements (Chandler and Fayet, 1993) and orf 1a/1b of astroviruses (Marczinke et al., 1994).
evidence: This is speculation based on the current findings and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Transient occlusion of the A site by an mRNA hairpin may underlie programmed ribosome pausing/stalling events that trigger targeting a nascent polypeptide chain to a membrane.
source: Transient occlusion of the A site by an mRNA hairpin may also underlie programmed ribosome pausing/stalling events that trigger targeting a nascent polypeptide chain to a membrane (Young and Andrews, 1996) and No-Go mRNA decay (Doma and Parker, 2006).
evidence: This is speculation based on the current findings and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Transient occlusion of the A site by an mRNA hairpin may underlie No-Go mRNA decay.
source: Transient occlusion of the A site by an mRNA hairpin may also underlie programmed ribosome pausing/stalling events that trigger targeting a nascent polypeptide chain to a membrane (Young and Andrews, 1996) and No-Go mRNA decay (Doma and Parker, 2006).
evidence: This is speculation based on the current findings and supported by citations to previous studies.
